Executive Summary

The NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) provides a flexible, outcome-based structure for managing cybersecurity risk across organisations of different sizes, sectors, and levels of maturity. This document provides a practical template for defining the organisation’s cybersecurity governance model, risk management approach, control structure, implementation roadmap, and assurance model using NIST CSF 2.0.

This template can be used to document the organisation’s target operating model for cybersecurity, align business and technology stakeholders, support risk-based investment decisions, and integrate cybersecurity with enterprise governance, resilience, compliance, and assurance processes.

Overview

Purpose

This document provides a practical template for defining, implementing, operating, and assuring a cybersecurity management system aligned to the NIST Cybersecurity Framework.

Objectives

The main objectives of applying the NIST Cybersecurity Framework are to:

  • establish a common language for cybersecurity risk
  • align cybersecurity with business objectives and enterprise risk
  • define and prioritise cybersecurity outcomes
  • improve governance, resilience, and incident readiness
  • strengthen communication across executives, business units, risk teams, and technical teams
  • support continuous improvement through profiles, tiers, metrics, and assurance

Scope

Describe the scope of NIST CSF applicability in the organisation.

In scope

  • enterprise cybersecurity governance
  • business services and critical processes
  • information assets and data
  • applications, platforms, infrastructure, and cloud services
  • operational technology where applicable
  • third-party services and supply chain dependencies
  • cyber resilience, incident response, and recovery arrangements

Out of scope

Document justified exclusions, if any.

Intended Audience

  • Board and executive leadership
  • Chief Information Security Officer
  • Chief Information Officer
  • Enterprise Risk Management teams
  • Security architecture and engineering teams
  • IT operations and service management teams
  • Business owners and control owners
  • Compliance and legal teams
  • Internal audit and assurance teams
  • PMO / transformation teams

Framework Foundation

Background

The NIST Cybersecurity Framework is designed to help organisations understand, assess, prioritise, and communicate cybersecurity risks. CSF 2.0 is intended for use by any organisation and is structured around six Functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover.

Core Components

The framework is built around the following components:

  • Functions
  • Categories
  • Subcategories
  • Organisational Profiles
  • Implementation Tiers

Profiles support comparison between current and target cybersecurity outcomes, and Tiers help characterise how rigorously cybersecurity risk governance and management practices are applied.

Functions

Document how the organisation applies the six CSF Functions:

  • Govern
  • Identify
  • Protect
  • Detect
  • Respond
  • Recover

Function summary

Function Purpose
Govern Establish, communicate, and monitor cybersecurity risk management strategy, expectations, and oversight
Identify Understand assets, business context, and cybersecurity risks
Protect Safeguard assets and reduce the likelihood or impact of incidents
Detect Discover and analyse anomalous events and cybersecurity incidents
Respond Contain, manage, and communicate during cybersecurity incidents
Recover Restore capabilities and services and improve resilience after incidents

Governance Model

Governance Objectives

Define the governance objectives for NIST CSF adoption:

  • establish executive accountability for cybersecurity risk
  • align cybersecurity priorities with enterprise strategy and risk appetite
  • assign ownership for CSF outcomes
  • embed governance into investment, change, operations, and resilience processes
  • maintain evidence of implementation and control effectiveness
  • support continuous improvement through profiles, metrics, and assurance

Governance Structure

Describe the governance bodies and their responsibilities.

Example governance bodies

  • Board / Risk Committee
  • Executive Cybersecurity Steering Committee
  • Information Security Forum
  • Enterprise Risk Committee
  • Architecture Review Board
  • Operational Resilience Committee
  • Internal Audit

Three Lines Model

Describe responsibilities across the three lines.

First line

  • business ownership of services, assets, and operational controls
  • technology and security operations
  • process execution and evidence production
  • incident detection, response, and recovery execution

Second line

  • cybersecurity governance
  • risk oversight
  • policy and standard setting
  • compliance monitoring
  • challenge and advisory support

Third line

  • internal audit
  • independent assurance
  • control effectiveness review

Standards and Procedures

Document the standards, baselines, procedures, and playbooks supporting implementation.

Core Processes

Govern

Describe how the organisation establishes cybersecurity strategy, policy, oversight, risk tolerance, roles, supply chain governance, and performance monitoring. CSF 2.0 introduced Govern as a distinct Function to strengthen governance and enterprise alignment. :contentReferenceoaicite:3

Identify

Describe the processes for:

  • asset inventory
  • business context analysis
  • dependency mapping
  • critical service identification
  • risk assessment
  • threat and vulnerability understanding

Protect

Describe the processes for:

  • access control
  • awareness and training
  • data protection
  • platform and infrastructure hardening
  • secure configuration
  • maintenance
  • protective technology
  • secure development and change management

Detect

Describe the processes for:

  • continuous monitoring
  • telemetry and log collection
  • alerting
  • anomaly detection
  • detection engineering
  • threat intelligence integration
  • triage and escalation

Respond

Describe the processes for:

  • incident triage
  • containment
  • eradication
  • internal and external communications
  • stakeholder coordination
  • regulatory notification where required
  • lessons learned

NIST’s incident response guidance aligns incident response activities with the CSF 2.0 functions and lifecycle. :contentReferenceoaicite:4

Recover

Describe the processes for:

  • restoration of services
  • recovery prioritisation
  • validation and assurance
  • resilience testing
  • crisis communications
  • recovery lessons learned
  • improvement planning

Sample Control Catalogue

Control ID Control Name Objective Control Owner Frequency Evidence
NIST-01 Cybersecurity strategy approved Ensure executive direction and accountability CISO Annual Approved strategy
NIST-02 Current and target profiles maintained Drive risk-based improvement Cyber Governance Lead Semi-annual Profile register
NIST-03 Asset inventory maintained Ensure visibility of assets and services IT Operations Monthly Asset register
NIST-04 Security monitoring performed Detect suspicious events in a timely manner SOC Manager Continuous SIEM reports
NIST-05 Incident response exercised Improve response readiness Incident Manager Quarterly Exercise reports
NIST-06 Recovery capabilities tested Validate resilience and restoration Continuity Lead Annual Recovery test evidence

  • identity compromise
  • unpatched vulnerabilities
  • supply chain exposure
  • insufficient monitoring coverage
  • weak incident coordination
  • inadequate resilience and recovery

  • poor evidence and assurance

Metrics and Reporting

Key Metrics

Examples of cybersecurity metrics:

  • percentage of critical assets identified

  • percentage of systems compliant with baseline configuration
  • vulnerability remediation performance
  • identity and privileged access review completion
  • mean time to detect
  • mean time to contain
  • mean time to recover
  • number of severe incidents
  • percentage of critical third parties assessed
  • percentage of recovery tests passed
  • percentage of target profile outcomes achieved

Implementation Roadmap

Maturity Phases

Phase 1: Foundation

  • establish governance and executive sponsorship
  • define policy framework
  • identify critical services and assets
  • create initial current profile
  • establish cyber risk register

Phase 2: Control Design

  • define target profile
  • prioritise control improvements
  • strengthen identity, monitoring, vulnerability, and response capabilities
  • define resilience and recovery expectations

Phase 3: Integration

  • integrate cyber governance with enterprise risk and architecture
  • align security operations with business service priorities
  • embed third-party and supply chain controls
  • improve playbooks, exercises, and evidence management

Phase 4: Optimisation

  • refine metrics and dashboards
  • automate control evidence
  • strengthen profile-based planning
  • expand resilience testing and assurance
  • drive continuous improvement

Maturity Model

Suggested Maturity Levels

Level 1: Initial

Cybersecurity activities are reactive, fragmented, and poorly governed.

Level 2: Repeatable

Basic practices exist but are inconsistently applied across the enterprise.

Level 3: Defined

Profiles, roles, controls, and processes are documented and broadly implemented.

Level 4: Managed

Cybersecurity activities are measured, risk-based, and regularly reviewed by leadership.

Level 5: Optimised

Cybersecurity is integrated into enterprise governance, architecture, operations, and resilience with continuous improvement and strong evidence.
